label: MODEL ESTIMATE: typical values for planning, not measurements
source: Typical estimates only. Frequency scaling follows free-space loss, 20*log10(f/2.4 GHz). Material attenuation values are rounded typical figures in the range reported by ITU-R P.2040 (building material properties) and published indoor measurements (for example NIST and vendor site-survey guides). Real walls vary by thickness, moisture, reinforcement and construction, so calibrate with a site survey before relying on them. Rate tables are typical 802.11n/ac/ax minimum-sensitivity style figures for one spatial stream, not vendor guarantees.

glass.label: Glass
sources: ITU-R P.2040 (effects of building materials and structures on radiowave propagation above about 100 MHz)
Published indoor measurements and vendor site-survey guides, summarised as rounded typical values
glass.notes: Plain single or double glazing. Low-emissivity or metal-coated glass can exceed 20 dB and is not covered, add it as a custom material.

drywall.label: Drywall
sources: ITU-R P.2040 (effects of building materials and structures on radiowave propagation above about 100 MHz)
Published indoor measurements and vendor site-survey guides, summarised as rounded typical values
drywall.notes: Single or double plasterboard on studs. Insulation or foil backing raises the loss.

wood.label: Wood
sources: ITU-R P.2040 (effects of building materials and structures on radiowave propagation above about 100 MHz)
Published indoor measurements and vendor site-survey guides, summarised as rounded typical values
wood.notes: Solid timber or timber stud partitions. Thickness and moisture content change the loss.

brick.label: Brick
sources: ITU-R P.2040 (effects of building materials and structures on radiowave propagation above about 100 MHz)
Published indoor measurements and vendor site-survey guides, summarised as rounded typical values
brick.notes: Single-leaf brick or block wall. Plaster, cavities and thickness move the loss within the range.

concrete.label: Concrete
sources: ITU-R P.2040 (effects of building materials and structures on radiowave propagation above about 100 MHz)
Published indoor measurements and vendor site-survey guides, summarised as rounded typical values
concrete.notes: Plain concrete or dense block wall without dense reinforcement.

metal.label: Metal
sources: ITU-R P.2040 (effects of building materials and structures on radiowave propagation above about 100 MHz)
Published indoor measurements and vendor site-survey guides, summarised as rounded typical values
metal.notes: Sheet metal, lift shafts, foil-backed panels. Close to total blockage, the measured loss is set by leakage at gaps and edges.

reinforced_concrete.label: Reinforced concrete
sources: ITU-R P.2040 (effects of building materials and structures on radiowave propagation above about 100 MHz)
Published indoor measurements and vendor site-survey guides, summarised as rounded typical values
reinforced_concrete.notes: Concrete with steel reinforcement. The rebar mesh spacing relative to the wavelength dominates and varies a lot, so the range is wide.

stone.label: Stone
sources: ITU-R P.2040 (effects of building materials and structures on radiowave propagation above about 100 MHz)
Published indoor measurements and vendor site-survey guides, summarised as rounded typical values
stone.notes: Natural stone masonry. Thickness and porosity vary widely.

plaster.label: Plaster
sources: ITU-R P.2040 (effects of building materials and structures on radiowave propagation above about 100 MHz)
Published indoor measurements and vendor site-survey guides, summarised as rounded typical values
plaster.notes: Plaster or render on lath or thin masonry backing. A wire mesh or metal lath backing raises the loss well above the typical value.

insulation.label: Insulation
sources: ITU-R P.2040 (effects of building materials and structures on radiowave propagation above about 100 MHz)
Published indoor measurements and vendor site-survey guides, summarised as rounded typical values
insulation.notes: Mineral wool or foam insulation panel without a metal facing. Foil-faced insulation behaves like a thin metal sheet and loses much more, so model it with the metal material.

office_partition.label: Office partition
sources: ITU-R P.2040 (effects of building materials and structures on radiowave propagation above about 100 MHz)
Published indoor measurements and vendor site-survey guides, summarised as rounded typical values
office_partition.notes: Modular office partition of fabric or laminate panels on a light frame, typically 1 to 2 m high screens up to full-height glazed partitions. Full-height steel-framed partitions lose more.

industrial_wall.label: Industrial wall
sources: ITU-R P.2040 (effects of building materials and structures on radiowave propagation above about 100 MHz)
Published indoor measurements and vendor site-survey guides, summarised as rounded typical values
industrial_wall.notes: Thick concrete block, precast panel or corrugated steel cladding of a factory or warehouse. The range is wide because cladding, racking and stored goods change the loss; use the metal material for a solid steel sheet.

steel.label: Steel
sources: ITU-R P.2040 (effects of building materials and structures on radiowave propagation above about 100 MHz)
Published indoor measurements and vendor site-survey guides, summarised as rounded typical values
steel.notes: Structural steel plate, beams and heavy cladding. Effectively a blocker, the measured loss is set by leakage at joints, gaps and openings, not by the steel itself.

aluminium.label: Aluminium
sources: ITU-R P.2040 (effects of building materials and structures on radiowave propagation above about 100 MHz)
Published indoor measurements and vendor site-survey guides, summarised as rounded typical values
aluminium.notes: Aluminium sheet, window frames, curtain wall mullions and foil-backed boards. Thin sheet leaks at edges, so the range is wide.

tiles.label: Tiles
sources: ITU-R P.2040 (effects of building materials and structures on radiowave propagation above about 100 MHz)
Published indoor measurements and vendor site-survey guides, summarised as rounded typical values
tiles.notes: Ceramic or stone tile on a masonry or board backing, as in bathrooms and kitchens. The tile layer adds a few dB over the bare backing, the backing sets most of the loss.

insulated_wall.label: Insulated wall
sources: ITU-R P.2040 (effects of building materials and structures on radiowave propagation above about 100 MHz)
Published indoor measurements and vendor site-survey guides, summarised as rounded typical values
insulated_wall.notes: Stud wall with mineral wool or foam insulation and plasterboard on both sides. Foil-faced insulation raises the loss towards the upper end of the range.

metal_door.label: Metal door
sources: ITU-R P.2040 (effects of building materials and structures on radiowave propagation above about 100 MHz)
Published indoor measurements and vendor site-survey guides, summarised as rounded typical values
metal_door.notes: Steel or aluminium skinned door in a frame. Loss is lower than the solid metal wall because of gaps around the leaf, a closed door is assumed.

fire_door.label: Fire door
sources: ITU-R P.2040 (effects of building materials and structures on radiowave propagation above about 100 MHz)
Published indoor measurements and vendor site-survey guides, summarised as rounded typical values
fire_door.notes: Fire-rated door with a steel skin, mineral core and a closed frame. Between a wooden door and a metal door, a closed door is assumed.

flooring.label: Flooring
sources: ITU-R P.2040 (effects of building materials and structures on radiowave propagation above about 100 MHz)
Published indoor measurements and vendor site-survey guides, summarised as rounded typical values
ITU-R P.1238 (indoor propagation, floor penetration loss) for the floor-loss context
flooring.notes: Light timber or composite floor build-up. The 2D engine applies floors as a fixed floor_loss_db per floor crossed, this entry is a reference for that value and for a future 3D model. Selecting it for a wall models a thin partition.

roofing.label: Roofing
sources: ITU-R P.2040 (effects of building materials and structures on radiowave propagation above about 100 MHz)
Published indoor measurements and vendor site-survey guides, summarised as rounded typical values
ITU-R P.1238 (indoor propagation, floor penetration loss) for the floor-loss context
roofing.notes: Tiles or sheet over timber, no metal foil. Foil-backed or metal roofing is much higher. The 2D engine has no roof, this entry is a reference for a future 3D model. Selecting it for a wall models a thin partition.

wifi_standards.label: MODEL ESTIMATE: PHY rates follow the IEEE 802.11 OFDM formula, minimum-SNR values are typical planning figures
wifi_standards.source: PHY rate = data subcarriers x bits per subcarrier x coding rate x spatial streams / symbol time (IEEE 802.11n-2009 clause 20, 802.11ac-2013 clause 21, 802.11ax-2021 clause 27, 802.11be-2024 clause 36). Data subcarrier counts and symbol times are the per-standard OFDM numerology of those clauses. Minimum-SNR per MCS are rounded typical planning figures (the standards normative receiver minimum sensitivity is a dBm value per MCS, not an SNR), not vendor guarantees. 802.11ac MCS 9 is not defined for every width and stream count, this model ignores that restriction.

mlo.label: CAPACITY MODEL, not a measurement: Multi-Link Operation (IEEE 802.11be-2024) aggregates the rates of the links, real gains depend on the client, the MLO mode and the traffic

interference.label: MODEL ESTIMATE: SINR from co-channel and adjacent-channel interference, a planning aid
interference.source: Thermal noise density -174 dBm/Hz at 290 K (kT, Johnson-Nyquist). Channel centres follow the IEEE 802.11 channel numbering (centre MHz = base + 5 x channel). The adjacent-channel rejection table is rounded from the IEEE 802.11 OFDM transmit spectrum mask for 20 MHz (about -20 dBr at 11 MHz, -28 dBr at 20 MHz and -40 dBr at 30 MHz from the centre), applied to the gap between the edges of the two occupied bandwidths. The noise figure and the activity factor are planning assumptions.

antenna.label: MODEL ESTIMATE: horizontal antenna pattern in the plan plane, no elevation, polarisation or near-field effects
antenna.source: The sector pattern is the 3GPP TR 36.814 horizontal pattern A(phi) = -min(12 (phi / phi_3dB)^2, A_m), phi_3dB the 3 dB beamwidth and A_m the front-to-back ratio. Azimuth 0 points along +x (east) and increases towards +y (south, clockwise on the plan).

external_sources.label: MODEL ESTIMATE: non-WiFi and neighbouring interference sources, planning assumptions, not measurements
external_sources.source: Each source is a spectrally flat emitter: its power is spread evenly over width_mhz around centre_mhz and the share that lands inside the victim receive band is overlap / width_mhz, scaled by duty_cycle. Microwave oven: a magnetron oven runs from half-wave rectified mains and radiates during about half of each mains cycle (the commonly cited 50 percent duty cycle), around 2.45 GHz inside the 2.4 to 2.5 GHz ISM band; the 50 MHz width and the 10 dBm effective leakage level are planning assumptions (ovens are limited by leakage rules, FCC 21 CFR 1030.10 and IEC 60335-2-25, not by a radiated spectrum mask). Bluetooth: 79 channels of 1 MHz from 2402 to 2480 MHz (Bluetooth Core Specification, BR/EDR hopping), class 2 maximum 2.5 mW (4 dBm); hopping is modelled as the average spread over the 78 MHz hop set, so a 20 MHz WiFi channel sees about 20/78 of the power; the duty cycle is a planning assumption for a connected audio or data link. Neighbour WiFi: a co-located network is treated like an AP of this project (same channel coupling and rejection table) with its own duty_cycle, a planning assumption for typical residential traffic. Non-WiFi sources have no adjacent-channel skirt.

reliability.label: ESTIMATE: airtime, latency and packet loss follow from SINR through an assumed PER curve. There is no standard formula, treat the numbers as indications, not measurements
reliability.source: PER(sinr) is a logistic curve 1 / (1 + exp((sinr - min_snr) / per_scale_db + ln((1 - per_at_min_snr) / per_at_min_snr))) around the MCS minimum SNR, so PER equals per_at_min_snr at that SNR. The 10 percent point follows the IEEE 802.11 receiver minimum sensitivity definition (PER 10 percent for a 1000 octet PSDU). per_scale_db sets how fast PER falls, a planning assumption. The MCS is the highest one the SINR supports. Packets are retried up to retry_limit times (IEEE 802.11 dot11ShortRetryLimit default 7), so the loss after retries is PER^(retry_limit + 1) and the mean transmissions are the sum of PER^k for k up to retry_limit. Latency = base_latency_ms + retries x retry_penalty_ms + busy / (1 - busy) x medium_wait_ms, with busy the share of time the serving AP hears non-WiFi or neighbour sources above the carrier sense level. base_latency_ms, retry_penalty_ms and medium_wait_ms are planning assumptions. Airtime is the share of the channel one client at the demand rate needs: demand / (PHY rate x MAC efficiency x (1 - PER) x (1 - busy)).

voids.label: MODEL ESTIMATE: stairwell and atrium openings reduce the floor loss locally, a planning approximation of the 2D plan
voids.source: A void is an optional polygon or rectangle on a floor where the slab is open (stairwell, lift shaft, atrium). The 2D model has no slab geometry, so the floor loss between two floors is scaled down by open_end_reduction for every end of the path (the AP, the receiver) that lies inside a void on its own floor. With both ends inside a void the floor loss is removed (reduction capped at 1). open_end_reduction is a planning assumption; real stairwells with doors or balustrades differ.

wall_thickness.label: MODEL ESTIMATE: wall loss scales linearly with thickness, a planning approximation, not a measurement
wall_thickness.source: The sourced attenuation_db of a material is the loss of a wall of that material at its reference thickness (reference_cm: a typical built thickness, a planning assumption). A wall with thickness_cm t loses attenuation_db x min(t / reference_cm, max_factor). Loss grows roughly linearly with the length of the path through a homogeneous material (ITU-R P.2040 models a slab by its attenuation per unit thickness), so the rule is linear; max_factor caps it because the straight-path model does not hold for very thick masses. A wall without thickness_cm loses exactly attenuation_db. Custom materials use default_reference_cm. Openings (doors, windows) keep their own loss and ignore thickness.

objects.label: MODEL ESTIMATE: furniture and metal objects are drawn as four wall segments, so a path through one crosses two edges
objects.source: An object is a rectangle of wall segments (kind interior, tagged with an object id) that reuses the wall loss pipeline, so no second loss path exists. Each edge carries the loss of its material at thickness_cm. A straight path through the rectangle crosses two edges, so the loss through an object is twice the edge loss. The default thickness_cm per kind is a planning assumption for the edge thickness, not the real depth of the furniture. Objects only attenuate paths that cross them in the 2D model and do not change the 3D heights.

spectrum.label: ESTIMATE: channel congestion from the access points and sources of the project, a planning aid, not a scan of the air
spectrum.source: Congestion of a channel is the sum over every AP and source in the project of coupling x duty cycle, where coupling is the share of the source power that lands in the candidate channel (interference.rejection_table for WiFi, spectral overlap for non-WiFi sources). It ignores distance, so it counts every source as if heard. APs use interference.activity_factor as duty cycle. Levels are thresholds on the congestion value, planning assumptions. On 2.4 GHz only the non-overlapping channels in preferred_channels are suggested.

decay.label: ESTIMATE: signal decay along a ray from an AP, from the same propagation model as the coverage map

timeline.label: ESTIMATE: signal along a walking path with a simple client roaming rule, not a measurement of any real client
timeline.source: The path is sampled every step_m metres along each straight segment (plus every waypoint). At each sample the engine gives the level of every AP. The client stays on its serving AP until a stronger AP is at least analytics.roam_min_dbm and either the serving AP has fallen below analytics.roam_min_dbm or the stronger AP beats it by hysteresis_db. A sample is in a handoff zone when the two strongest APs are both at least analytics.roam_min_dbm and within analytics.roam_margin_db, the same rule as the roaming map. Real clients use vendor specific roaming thresholds and scan timing that are not modelled.

recommendations.label: ESTIMATE: ranked actions, every delta is the difference between two runs of the same propagation model, confidence is model sensitivity not accuracy
recommendations.source: The coverage score out of 100 is the weighted mean of the coverage percentage, the share of the floor that is not a dead zone and the mean throughput against throughput_full_mbps. Each action is applied to a copy of the project and the analytics of both are compared, so every delta is measured. Actions are ranked by score delta, then by id. Actions that do not raise the score by at least min_score_gain are dropped. Confidence is the share of wall attenuation perturbations (planner.confidence) under which the action still raises the score.

design.label: ESTIMATE: generated network plan from the planner placement search, a starting point to verify with a site survey

roaming.label: ESTIMATE: exact per-cell roaming data from the strongest and second strongest AP, the blend is a planning aid, not a client roaming simulation
roaming.source: Per cell: the strongest AP, the second AP, the margin between them and a zone. Zone handoff: both APs at least analytics.roam_min_dbm and the margin at most analytics.roam_margin_db. Zone overlap: a second AP at least analytics.overlap_min_dbm within analytics.overlap_margin_db of the strongest. Else single. Blend is the share of the cell notionally served by the strongest AP: 50 percent at zero margin rising linearly to 100 percent at analytics.roam_margin_db. Client roaming thresholds and stickiness are not modelled.

scoring.label: Optimisation score, a weighted sum of estimates, higher is better. Weights are planning preferences, not physics.

planner.label: Smart WiFi Planner settings. Recommendations are model estimates, confidence expresses model sensitivity, not real-world accuracy.

planner_modes.label: ESTIMATE: planning aids built on the propagation model, typical values, not measurements

planner_layers.label: ESTIMATE: map layers derived from the propagation model, a planning aid, not measurements
planner_layers.source: Each layer is a per-cell value over the analysis grid. Layers that need an AP with a WiFi standard (SINR, latency, packet loss, interference) come from the SINR and reliability sections of the analysis (docs/platform/15-wifi-physics.md). SNR is the best RSSI minus the thermal plus noise-figure floor of the serving AP width. Wall attenuation is the best RSSI computed with the walls of the floor removed minus the best RSSI with them, so it is the loss the walls and openings add. Quality score blends the signal position between the dead zone level and the best quality band edge with the throughput position between 0 and bandwidth.hi, using quality_weights, planning preferences not physics. Channel utilisation and capacity are those of the serving AP in the analytics section. The ranges lo and hi map a value onto the colour scale, higher_is_better flips it so that a good value is always the strong end of the scale.

dashboard.efficiency_note: Efficiency score is the average over cells of min(1, estimated bandwidth / efficiency_target_mbps), in percent. The target is a planning assumption.

editor.label: Editing defaults for doors, windows and floor openings, drawing conveniences, not physics

floor_elevation.label: MODEL ESTIMATE: floor-to-floor loss scales with the elevation difference when both floors set elevation_m, not a measurement
floor_elevation.source: Floor loss per floor is a typical figure for a slab of about reference_height_m floor-to-floor height. A floor pair that sets elevation_m on both floors crosses |elevation difference| / reference_height_m floors, at least one. Floors without elevation_m keep the whole-floor count from their level, so saved projects are unchanged. Basements have negative elevation_m.

ap_profiles.label: Typical generic router and access point classes, not product names, planning values only
ap_profiles.source: Each profile is a typical class of consumer, gaming, mesh and enterprise Wi-Fi equipment, not a specific product. Transmit power per band is chosen so that tx_dbm plus antenna_gain_dbi stays within the ETSI EIRP limit of that band (EN 300 328 for 2.4 GHz at 20 dBm, EN 301 893 for 5 GHz at 23 dBm in the lower 5 GHz sub-bands, EN 303 687 for 6 GHz low power indoor at 23 dBm). FCC limits are higher, so the profiles also meet them. Limits are approximate, check the current regulation of the country before deploying.

consumer.label: Consumer router
consumer.description: Typical home router class: dual band, two spatial streams, small integrated antennas.

gaming.label: Gaming router
gaming.description: Typical high end home router class: tri band, four spatial streams, larger antennas.

mesh.label: Mesh node
mesh.description: Typical mesh satellite class: tri band, two spatial streams, a dedicated backhaul radio is not modelled.

enterprise.label: Enterprise access point
enterprise.description: Typical ceiling mounted enterprise AP class: tri band, four spatial streams, omnidirectional ceiling antenna.

client_devices.label: MODEL ESTIMATE: typical sustained demand of common Smart Home client classes, not measurements
client_devices.source: Demand is a typical sustained figure: 1080p IP camera 2 to 6 Mbps, 4K streaming TV about 25 Mbps (streaming services recommend 15 to 25 Mbps), phone video call and browsing about 5 Mbps, console game download and stream mix about 15 Mbps, IoT sensor under 1 Mbps, video doorbell about 3 Mbps (a 1080p stream like the IP camera, upload only), smart speaker music streaming about 0.4 Mbps (320 kbps high quality audio), thermostat under 0.1 Mbps (small status messages), robot vacuum about 1 Mbps (map and app video, planning assumption). Bands are the typical radio support of the class, many cameras, doorbells, thermostats, vacuums and IoT devices are 2.4 GHz only.

capacity_models.label: CAPACITY MODEL, not a measurement: OFDMA, MU-MIMO and beamforming are simple planning models of their typical gain, real gains depend on the client, the traffic and the driver
capacity_models.source: OFDMA (IEEE 802.11ax-2021 and 802.11be) splits a channel into resource units so that small frames of several clients share one transmission, the gain grows with the number of clients and saturates. DL MU-MIMO (802.11ac wave 2 and later) serves several clients at once with separate spatial streams, each extra client adds spatial_efficiency of one client of capacity. Beamforming focuses the transmit pattern towards a client, modelled as array gain of array_gain_db_per_doubling for each doubling of the stream count, scaled by steering_efficiency and capped at max_gain_db. The numeric values are planning assumptions of low confidence, not taken from a measurement campaign.

planner_3d.label: MODEL ESTIMATE: the 3D view stacks the per-floor 2D results and interpolates between floors, it is not a 3D propagation simulation
planner_3d.source: Floors sit at elevation_m, or at level times floor_elevation.reference_height_m when elevation_m is not set. A slice between two floors blends the two 2D RSSI grids linearly in dB with the height fraction. The per-floor grids already include the engine floor loss (floor_loss_db and floor_elevation), so the blend shows a plausible trend between floors and is not a computed field. Nothing is extrapolated above the top floor or below the lowest. The access point marker height and the steered beam width are drawing assumptions.

compare.label: MODEL ESTIMATE: the generation table uses the engine path loss, noise floor and OFDM rate formulas for one reference link, it is not a product benchmark

insight.label: ESTIMATE: room analysis, gaming ping, grades and assistant diagnoses are scoring layers over the propagation model, not measurements
insight.source: Every number shown comes from the engine grids (RSSI, SINR, throughput, packet error, loss after retries, latency, airtime from linkReliability) averaged over the cells whose centre lies in a room. The values here only decide how those numbers are mapped to words and grades; they are planning assumptions, not standards. There is no standard formula from RSSI to ping, so ping is always a range: isp_base_ms (user adjustable, a typical fixed broadband round trip to a regional game server, roughly 10 to 30 ms) plus round_trip_factor times the engine Wi-Fi latency between the range_low_percentile and range_high_percentile of the room cells (the Wi-Fi hop is crossed twice in a round trip). Jitter proxy = round_trip_factor x the same percentile spread of the latency plus airtime_jitter_ms x the airtime share. Packet loss risk is Low, Medium or High from the worse of the loss after retries and the first attempt packet error (10 percent is the IEEE 802.11 receiver minimum sensitivity definition). Gaming stability = 100 x the weighted mean of four components (ping, jitter, loss, signal margin), each falling linearly from 1 at its full value to 0 at its zero value, times the share of room cells that are not dead. The ping, jitter and loss bounds follow common interactive voice and video guidance (ITU-T G.114 one way delay under 150 ms, jitter under 30 ms, loss under 1 percent) tightened for games. Streaming needs about 25 Mbps per 4K stream (streaming services recommend 15 to 25 Mbps), judged at the throughput_percentile of the room cells so the weak corners count. Video calls need about 4 Mbps for an HD call plus low latency and loss; the weakest component sets the score. Grades and rating words use the minimum scores listed. The mesh model keeps the engine coverage and applies the existing planner_modes.mesh.hop_throughput_factor per wireless hop to throughput plus hop_latency_ms of extra latency per hop, an assumption for a shared band backhaul. The assistant is a deterministic keyword parser, not a language model.

signal_waves.label: ILLUSTRATION: animated rings drawn from each access point, dimmed after every wall using the engine wall loss. A picture of how walls absorb signal, not a measured wavefront
signal_waves.source: Each ring is sampled along rays from the access point. A ray accumulates the loss of the walls and openings it crosses with the engine wallLoss (the same value the heat map uses at that radius) and the ring brightness falls linearly to zero at fade_loss_db of accumulated loss. fade_loss_db 30 dB is a drawing choice: a ray that has lost 30 dB is shown as almost invisible. Speed, ring spacing and ray counts are presentation settings chosen for a readable animation on a Raspberry Pi 4, not physical values (radio waves move at the speed of light). The ray count follows the page quality setting.
